$comment: How many of the 10,000 MNIST test predictions change when the committed double
checkpoint is replaced by the float32 export the browser actually downloads?
benchmarks/mnist_eval.json records 9701/10000 = 97.01% from model.weights, the
800,678-byte ASCII checkpoint at full double precision. The landing page's wasm
path fetches web/public/wasm/model.weights.bin instead -- the 318,064-byte float32
export written by apps/export_weights.cpp -- and widens it back to double on load.
If those two disagree, re-running the accuracy claim in a visitor's browser is not
a reproduction of the claim.
Produced by: fast_mnist_eval model.weights data TestingSetList.txt benchmarks --f32-weights
after: cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build --target fast_mnist_eval. The f32
network is loaded from the shipped .bin through NeuralNet::loadBinary, not re-derived;
parameter_check below verifies element by element that those bytes are exactly
static_cast<double>(static_cast<float>(w)) of the ASCII checkpoint.
LIMITATION -- this is the QUANTISATION difference only, and it does not bound the
true browser-vs-native delta. Both columns here were computed by the same native
kernel, so two further differences are unmeasured: (1) reduction order -- the arm64
NEON path in src/NeuralNet.cpp accumulates in one f64x2 accumulator and reduces two
lanes, while the wasm simd128 path uses two independent f64x2 accumulators and
reduces four; and (2) FMA contraction -- the NEON kernel uses vfmaq_f64, so products
are never rounded, while wasm simd128 has no FMA and rounds every product. (2) is
plausibly the larger of the two, since it changes rounding at every multiply rather
than only in the reduction tree. The real browser-vs-native delta can therefore be
larger than the number below, and is not bounded by it. Measuring it requires
running the emscripten build itself and diffing against this native run.

parameter_check.note: every weight and bias in the .bin equals static_cast<double>(static_cast<float>(w)) of the ASCII value

flips.note: images whose argmax differs between the two weight precisions; helpful = f32 right where double was wrong

tightest_margins.note: the 10 smallest double-regime argmax margins (top1 - top2) in the test set -- the images most exposed to f32 rounding

spot_checks.note: indices named by hand as knife-edge errors; margin here is top1 - top2, which is not always pred - true
